collections.title: SaaS landing-page references
collections.description: Focused references for studying SaaS positioning, landing-page structure, pricing presentation, proof, copy, and conversion patterns.
collections.outcome: A defensible SaaS landing-page direction covering positioning, page structure, proof, and pricing.
collections.audience: Founders, product marketers, and designers preparing or revising a SaaS marketing site.

stages.title: Frame the market
stages.inspect: Compare positioning, information hierarchy, and recurring page structures before choosing a direction.
stages.decision: Choose which category conventions to follow, adapt, or deliberately reject.

items.role: SaaS Pages anchors the first scan with examples that combine visual structure and copywriting.
SaaSpo provides another curated market lens for identifying repeated conventions without treating them as rules.

stages.title: Assemble the page
stages.inspect: Inspect section-level composition, proof placement, copy patterns, and reusable landing-page structures.
stages.decision: Decide the page sequence and which sections deserve custom design versus established patterns.

items.role: Landingfolio helps inspect individual sections and templates before composing the full page.
Really Good Emails adds onboarding and lifecycle email references when the marketing journey extends beyond the homepage.

stages.title: Decide pricing presentation
stages.inspect: Study pricing architecture, plan comparison, and how price and proof are presented together.
stages.decision: Decide how to present price, plans, and proof before implementation.

items.role: Pricing Pages isolates pricing architecture, plan comparison, and purchase-friction patterns.

collections.title: Typography and font tools
collections.description: A practical starting set for finding typefaces, studying real typography and pairings, and exploring open and commercial font libraries.
collections.outcome: A practical typography direction with licensed candidate fonts, real-world references, pairing rationale, and implementation options.
collections.audience: Designers and frontend teams choosing type for a brand, marketing site, or product interface.

stages.title: Source viable candidates
stages.inspect: Start with broad, implementable libraries and distinguish open, free, and subscription options.
stages.decision: Choose the licensing and delivery boundary for the shortlist.

items.role: Google Fonts provides a broad web-ready baseline with straightforward delivery.
Fontshare offers free professional families that can raise the quality of the initial shortlist.
Typewolf supplies editorial recommendations, pairings seen on real sites, and category context for narrowing candidates.

stages.title: Study type in context
stages.inspect: Inspect real uses, editorial tone, hierarchy, and category conventions before judging isolated specimens.
stages.decision: Decide which type qualities support the intended brand and reading experience.

items.role: Fonts In Use shows typography in real artifacts rather than isolated specimen pages.
Free Faces adds a curated view of freely licensed typefaces.

stages.title: Finalize the shortlist
stages.inspect: Compare more distinctive open and commercial families once the core direction and pairings are clear.
stages.decision: Select the primary and supporting families to prototype and test.

items.role: Velvetyne introduces experimental libre options when the direction needs more character.
Adobe Fonts provides a subscription-backed comparison set for teams already using Creative Cloud.

collections.title: Motion starter pack
collections.description: A balanced introduction to interface animation, interactive vectors, JavaScript motion, WebGL, and browser-based 3D workflows.
collections.outcome: A motion approach matched to the interaction goal, runtime constraints, authoring workflow, and team stack.
collections.audience: Designers and frontend engineers deciding how to add purposeful interface motion, vector animation, or browser 3D.

stages.title: Define the motion scope
stages.inspect: Compare general-purpose animation libraries with automatic transitions to separate essential interaction feedback from spectacle.
stages.decision: Choose whether the project needs timeline control, lightweight transitions, or both.

items.role: Motion provides a production-oriented JavaScript and React baseline for interface animation.
GSAP represents high-control timeline animation when sequencing and performance are central.
LottieFiles supports asset-based vector animation workflows and handoff.

stages.title: Choose the asset workflow
stages.inspect: Inspect vector and browser-based 3D authoring workflows, runtime ownership, and handoff needs.
stages.decision: Decide whether motion should be authored as interactive vectors, 3D scenes, or code.

items.role: Rive adds stateful interactive vector animation rather than playback-only assets.
Spline provides a collaborative browser 3D authoring route for teams avoiding low-level scene code.
Three.js establishes the lower-level WebGL option and its engineering cost.

stages.title: Match the implementation stack
stages.inspect: Compare React integration for 3D with smaller code-driven animation libraries.
stages.decision: Select the implementation layer that fits the framework, performance budget, and maintenance capacity.

items.role: React Three Fiber shows how Three.js integrates with React component architecture.
Anime.js offers a smaller code-driven animation alternative for targeted interactions.

collections.title: Open-source UI libraries
collections.description: Open-source component systems and primitives for building accessible, composable, and implementation-ready web interfaces.
collections.outcome: A component-library strategy that balances accessibility, styling ownership, speed, animation needs, and long-term maintenance.
collections.audience: React product teams selecting primitives, copyable components, or higher-level UI building blocks.

stages.title: Choose the foundation
stages.inspect: Compare accessible primitives, hooks, and copy-owned components before evaluating visual libraries.
stages.decision: Decide how much behavior, styling, and source ownership the team wants.

items.role: shadcn/ui demonstrates copy-owned React components built on accessible primitives.
Radix UI represents unstyled accessible primitives with strong behavior ownership.

stages.title: Accelerate common UI
stages.inspect: Inspect accessible hooks and composable component sets that can extend the chosen foundation.
stages.decision: Decide which higher-level components are safe to adopt rather than rebuild.

items.role: React Aria provides accessibility-focused hooks and components for teams needing deeper behavior control.
Kibo UI extends shadcn-oriented projects with more composable application components.

stages.title: Add expression carefully
stages.inspect: Review community, interactive, and motion-heavy components only after the accessibility and ownership boundary is fixed.
stages.decision: Choose where expressive components add value without fragmenting the system.

items.role: Uiverse provides community-made visual elements that require selective quality review.
React Bits adds animated and interactive React components for targeted expressive moments.
Motion Primitives focuses specifically on reusable animated interface building blocks.

collections.title: Accessible colour tools
collections.description: Tools for building colour systems, checking contrast, understanding visual-access needs, and evaluating interface accessibility.
collections.outcome: A colour system that communicates the intended brand while surviving contrast, visual-impairment, and page-level checks.
collections.audience: Designers and frontend teams defining or auditing interface colour systems.

stages.title: Build the system
stages.inspect: Generate candidate palettes and scales with explicit accessibility constraints rather than choosing isolated swatches.
stages.decision: Choose the tonal structure and semantic colour roles to prototype.

items.role: Adobe Color supports early palette exploration and basic accessibility checks.
Leonardo helps generate adaptive, contrast-aware colour systems.
InclusiveColors creates WCAG-aware scales suitable for tokenized interfaces.

stages.title: Test human impact
stages.inspect: Inspect contrast ratios and how combinations affect people with different visual impairments.
stages.decision: Decide which colour pairs and text treatments are safe for the intended content.

items.role: Who Can Use translates contrast choices into human-impact context.
WebAIM Contrast Checker provides a focused standards-based foreground/background test.

stages.title: Verify in context
stages.inspect: Preview the system on interfaces, then run page-level accessibility checks.
stages.decision: Approve, revise, or reject the colour implementation based on contextual evidence.

items.role: Realtime Colors previews palette and typography choices in a page-like context.
WAVE provides a page-level evaluation lens for issues that automation and visual inspection reveal.

collections.title: Design systems worth studying
collections.description: Public design systems that demonstrate foundations, tokens, content guidance, accessibility, component architecture, and product-specific patterns.
collections.outcome: A documented set of design-system decisions grounded in relevant public systems rather than copied visual conventions.
collections.audience: Product designers, design-system teams, and frontend leads defining foundations, components, content, and governance.

stages.title: Compare foundations
stages.inspect: Study broad platform and enterprise systems to compare tokens, foundations, component scope, and documentation structure.
stages.decision: Choose the foundation categories and documentation depth the project actually needs.

items.role: Material Design 3 provides a broad reference for tokens, adaptive foundations, and component guidance.
Apple Human Interface Guidelines shows platform-specific interaction and presentation constraints.
IBM Carbon demonstrates enterprise component architecture and documentation breadth.

stages.title: Study product context
stages.inspect: Inspect systems shaped by commerce, collaboration, creative tools, and productivity products.
stages.decision: Decide which product-specific patterns transfer and which are context-bound.

items.role: Shopify Polaris shows a design system shaped by commerce workflows and product language.
Atlassian Design System provides patterns for dense collaborative software.
Adobe Spectrum demonstrates cross-platform consistency for creative applications.

stages.title: Learn from public-service rigor
stages.inspect: Review systems where accessibility, content, service consistency, and contribution governance are explicit.
stages.decision: Define the accessibility, content, and governance standards required for the project.

items.role: Microsoft Fluent 2 offers another large-scale foundation and component model.
GitHub Primer connects components, CSS, product patterns, and open contribution.
GOV.UK Design System foregrounds accessible service patterns, content, and evidence.
U.S. Web Design System adds public-sector tokens, components, and implementation guidance.
